lead: Celestial navigation rests on one picture: the sky as a sphere round you, each body standing over one spot on the Earth. From it comes the triangle every sight solves.

sections.title: The sky as a sphere round you

qa.q: How high above the horizon is the celestial pole at my latitude?
qa.a: As high as your latitude: the **elevated pole** P, the one above your horizon, stands at an altitude equal to your latitude. On the equator both poles lie on the horizon.

refs: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole
Celestial sphere — celestial and visible horizon

blocks.p: **Latitude** is the arc of your meridian from the equator to you; 1′ of it is one mile. **Longitude** is the arc of the equator from Greenwich to your meridian, east or west up to 180°.

Your **zenith** Z is the point overhead, the nadir the point underfoot. The **celestial horizon** is the great circle 90° from the zenith, through the Earth's centre; a sextant altitude is corrected to it first. Your **meridian** is the great circle through the celestial poles and your zenith.
The **elevated pole** P is the one above your horizon, as high as your latitude; on the equator both poles lie on the horizon.

fig.note: Meridian view · latitude 30°N · pole 30° above north

qa.q: How do I get the local hour angle from GHA and my longitude?
qa.a: **LHA** = GHA + east longitude, or − west longitude, ± 360°. Under 180° the body is west of you, past your meridian; over 180° it is east of you, still climbing.

blocks.p: The **geographical position** (GP) is the spot with the body in its zenith. Its latitude is the **declination** (Dec); its longitude comes from the **Greenwich hour angle** (GHA), measured westward from Greenwich through 360°: GHA west up to 180°, beyond that 360° − GHA east.
The Sun's GP runs west at 15° an hour: a watch 4 seconds out moves it, and your fix, 1′ of longitude. A wrong Dec moves it north or south.

fig.note: From above the north pole · west is clockwise

blocks.p: GHA and Dec are the same for every navigator. The **local hour angle** (LHA), measured westward from your own meridian, is yours alone: under 180° the body is west of you, past your meridian; over 180° it is east, still climbing.

blocks.rule: LHA = GHA + east longitude, or − west longitude (± 360°).

sections.title: One point for every star

qa.q: How do I find a star's GHA from the almanac?
qa.a: Add the star's **sidereal hour angle** (SHA) to the GHA of the First Point of Aries for that hour, and take off 360° if the sum is over: GHA star = GHA Aries + SHA.

refs: First point of Aries and SHA
First point of Aries — the sidereal day

blocks.p: The stars keep their places, so the almanac tabulates one point, the **First Point of Aries**, hour by hour and gives each star a fixed **sidereal hour angle** (SHA), measured westward from Aries. For a planet, GHA minus GHA Aries gives its SHA.

blocks.rule: GHA star = GHA Aries + SHA, less 360° if over.

fig.title: A star's GHA and LHA
lines: The star is west of your meridian

blocks.p: Against the stars the Earth turns in 23 h 56 min: a star crosses your meridian about 4 minutes earlier each night. The Moon slips east among the stars about 13° a day and crosses some 50 minutes later.

sections.title: Why the Sun's declination swings

qa.q: Why does the Sun's declination change through the year?
qa.a: Because the Sun's yearly path, the **ecliptic**, is tilted 23°26′ to the celestial equator. Its Dec is 0° at the equinoxes and 23°26′ north or south at the solstices, changing fastest near the equinoxes, about 24′ a day.

refs: Declination through the year — the ecliptic
The Sun's declination through the year

blocks.p: A star's Dec hardly changes. The Sun's does: its yearly path, the **ecliptic**, is tilted 23°26′ to the celestial equator. That tilt, not the distance to the Sun, makes the seasons.

Near the equinoxes the Dec changes fastest, about 24′ a day: the wrong day's figure costs miles. The Sun passes through your zenith only between the tropics, when its Dec equals your latitude; its bearing then swings from east to west within minutes of noon.

sections.title: The triangle behind every sight

qa.q: What are the sides of the PZX triangle, and what does solving it give?
qa.a: The **PZX triangle** joins the elevated pole, your zenith and the body: PZ is 90° − latitude, PX is 90° − Dec, or 90° + Dec for contrary names. Solving it gives ZX, hence Hc, and the azimuth.

refs: PZX triangle — the angle at P

blocks.p: Join the elevated pole P, your zenith Z and the body X by great circles. Knowing PZ, PX and the angle between them, you get ZX, hence the calculated altitude Hc, and the angle at Z, the azimuth. The angle at X is never used.

PX is 90° − Dec, or 90° + Dec when Dec and latitude have contrary names. South of the equator P is the south celestial pole. The azimuth angle Z is reckoned from the elevated pole, east or west, then turned into true azimuth Zn.

fig.title: Setting up the triangle
lines: Z from the tables: S 147° E

blocks.p: An absurd intercept usually means Dec named north for south.

sections.title: One sight, one circle

qa.q: How far am I from a body's geographical position, given its observed altitude?
qa.a: The **zenith distance**, 90° − Ho, at 60 miles to the degree: Ho 60° puts you 1800 miles from the GP, on a circle round it shared by everyone measuring that altitude at that instant.

refs: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance
Circle of equal altitude — position line
Circle of equal altitude — high-altitude sights
Circle of equal altitude — the assumed position

blocks.p: The **zenith distance**, 90° − Ho, is also your distance from the GP, 60 miles to the degree. Everyone measuring that altitude at that instant is on one circle round the GP: Ho 60° puts you 1800 miles from it.

fig.note: Two sights, two circles · you are where they cross near the DR

blocks.p: The circle is so large that near you its arc is a straight **position line**, at right angles to the azimuth. Compare Ho with Hc for an assumed position (AP): if Ho is greater you are nearer the GP, and the line moves towards the body by the difference in miles, whichever AP you chose. A body due east or west gives a north–south line: longitude.

fig.note: Plotting sheet, north up · intercept towards

blocks.p: For a very high Sun, above about 87°, you draw the circle round the GP itself. An altitude 1′ too high puts the line a mile too far towards the body.

sections.title: The daily path of a body

qa.q: When does a star never set at my latitude?
qa.a: When its Dec has the same name as your latitude and exceeds 90° − latitude: the body is **circumpolar**. With that Dec and the contrary name it never rises; on the equator everything rises and sets.

refs: Meridian altitude — why it gives latitude
Circumpolar bodies — upper and lower transit

blocks.p: A body is highest as it crosses your meridian, its GP then nearest to you. P, Z and X lie on one arc: the zenith distance is the difference between latitude and Dec, or their sum for contrary names, and the body bears north if its GP is north of you. So a noon sight gives latitude without tables.

A body whose Dec has the name of your latitude and exceeds 90° − latitude is **circumpolar**: it never sets, and at lower transit stands latitude + Dec − 90° high. With that Dec and the contrary name it never rises. On the equator everything rises and sets.

fig.note: Latitude 40°N · star Dec N60° · it never sets

blocks.p: A body with Dec 0° rises due east; with a north Dec, north of east in either hemisphere, staying up over 12 hours in north latitude.
